It will be recalled that yesterday during Question Period the member for Cape Breton-East Richmond was called to order on his references to the Governor General, and he was asked to withdraw those statements, which of course he did.
The unfortunate thing is that even though those comments were withdrawn, they ended up on the National last night at ten o'clock.
Once again, I think this draws to the attention of this Chamber how important it is that remarks which breach the traditions of this House, which make reference to the Governor General or to other individuals, that may well be slanderous, or something that could be in some way offensive, have to be dealt with very quickly and very efficiently.
What happens as a result of that withdrawn statement is that it continues to stay on the record. The net result is that the statement that was played on the National last night is I think a poor reflection on the House and the Governor General.

infer that Parliament had no role in the passage of this measure.

-the Hibernia bill has been passed.

I insist on bringing this press release and all related statements to your attention, because what happened was that they used Parliament as a rubber stamp. You yourself warned on October 10, 1989, that you would not be as generous next time.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to intervene for a couple of minutes. I want to indicate to the hon. member and to the House that, in fact, the Government of Canada has entered into an agreement with the Province of Newfoundland which is mutually acceptable to both levels of government.
I should also indicate to the hon. member that under the existing estimates, which were by this House at another time, the essential funds to start up the project have already been approved and are in place. So there is absolutely no discrepancy between what we, as members, are now dealing with in this House, that is, Bill C-44, and the fact that the announcements have proceeded and that things are going. I do not see any inconsistency at all. It is an interesting point of order but perhaps it should be better described as debate.
Mr. Speaker, so far this is a point of privilege. What my hon. friend-
A point of privilege?

He is arguing a point of privilege, Mr. Speaker. The point being made is that the government has prejudged what Parliament will do. We have seen this occur on previous occasions and on those occasions your rulings were very specific.
I agree with the comments made by my hon. friend earlier. I was surprised that legislation had been passed. In fact, it had not been passed when I heard a deal had

Business of the House
been made between the federal government, the provinces and the companies involved. It requires legislation to be passed.
I think it is fair to say that all of us take our work here very seriously. But when the government announces that it is going ahead with this project, it is simply assuming that, not only the House of Commons but the Senate will pass the legislation, I do not think that that assumption ought always to be made. As a matter of fact, the Senate is not even in session any longer. If the Senate were to do what it presumably plans to do, and that is to keep the bells ringing indefinitely, this legislation we are discussing now, Hibernia, would never occur.
When the government suggests that the project will go ahead and guarantees that legislation will be passed, that does not provide much incentive for us here in the House to take our job very seriously. So I simply want to summarize by saying that if the government wants the co-operation and support of the opposition parties, I think it is in their interest to recognize that there are stages through which legislation must pass. We are not even beyond report stage with the Hibernia legislation and from here it goes into the other House.
Time after time we have seen the present federal government consider Parliament to be a nuisance to their agenda. This adds to the public perception that this government would just as soon not have Parliament in session and simply announce their initiatives by decree.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to the arguments of the hon. member which, of course, were just a reiteration of what we had heard a few moments ago. It is the second day I have been obliged to raise matters with regard to the Minister of Finance. He was given notice that I intended to rise but did not choose to stay.
At the conclusion of Question Period he rose and referred to having said that I had deliberately misled the House in a question that I put to him. He said that he would withdraw the word "deliberately". He then proceeded to convey the impression that I had indeed misrepresented. The authorities are mixed on whether the word misrepresent is unparliamentary. In Beau-chesne's Fifth Edition it can be concluded that it is either unparliamentary, on page 109, where attempted to misrepresent has been found unparliamentary or, it has been accepted, as noted on page 112.
I feel it is necessary to make the point that I did not fail to check numbers, nor did I attempt to misrepresent in the question that I put. It was a question relating to the goods and services tax and the extent to which the tax will affect a shift in taxation in Canada from businesses to households. In the minister's own statements in this House in second reading debate, he said that it was $6 billion.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The issue was first raised by the hon. member for Ottawa South and raised immediately and properly with the Chair on the question of "deliberately misrepresent." There is no doubt in my mind that "deliberately misrepresent" is unparliamentary. The question of "mislead" or "misrepresent" may or may not be unparliamentary, depending on the context in which it is used. If it is an argument over facts, that goes on in this place all the time. If it is said, and it may well have been, in the matter that the hon. member quotes, it may have been said in a context in which the accusation was a very severe one indeed. That is why I caution hon. members not to just look in Beauchesne's to see what words have, at one time or another, been ruled as unparliamentary, but to remember that it also has to be considered in the context.
In this case, I understand the hon. member, who is a conscientious member in this place, wanting to establish that he did not make this statement carelessly. If the hon. minister has a view about it which is different than his own, that is a matter of debate. However, the hon.

Routine Proceedings
member has said that he feels that he made that in good faith. The hon. minister has withdrawn any suggestion that there was any deliberateness on the part of the hon. member and I think that that is where the matter must end.
Again, it is an example of how careful we do have to be, even in debate, and even in the rough and tumble of exchanges in this place.

speakeroldname: Mr. Albert Cooper (Parliamentary Secretary to Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 36(8), I have the honour to table, in both official languages, the Government's response to one petition.
[Editor's Note: See today's Votes and Proceedings.]

That the second report of the Standing Committee on Aboriginal Affairs, presented to the House on Thursday, March 29, 1990, be concurred in.
He said: Madam Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to take this opportunity to rise in the House and request that the House concur in the second report of the Standing Committee on Aboriginal Affairs.
As the House will be aware, the Standing Committee on Aboriginal Affairs, over the period of last winter and last spring, took it upon itself to interview leaders of the national and regional aboriginal organizations in order to develop an agenda that Parliament, the government and the people of Canada could deal with through the nineties, to address, as per the title of our report which is called The Unfinished Business Between Canada and its Aboriginal Peoples.
As a result of this investigation carried out by the standing committee, we identified an agenda of approximately 30 items, extremely complex and detailed items, identified thanks to the assistance of the aboriginal leadership of Canada. There were 30 items which represent the outstanding grievances of aboriginal people in Canada and also represent what aboriginal people would like to see dealt with in the 1990s.
It would be appropriate, although this is not one of the recommendations in the report, that Canada consider the decade of the nineties as the decade in which we, as Parliament and we as a people, commit ourselves to finishing that unfinished business remaining between us and our aboriginal people.
I understand that the government is required to respond to the reports of select standing committees within a certain period of time. I believe that period is 120 days. Well, 120 days has expired and what response have we received from the government on this detailed report, concurred in by all parties represented on that committee?
I will tell you how the government responded to that report, Madam Speaker. The Secretary of State for Canada cancelled funding for aboriginal representative organizations, cancelled funding for native communications, newspapers, reduced funding for organizations such as friendship centres and native broadcasting organizations. The government has consistently refused to set up an institute, again through the Secretary of State, to protect aboriginal languages which are dying out in this country at a great rate. Yet at the same time it set up an institute for heritage languages that have a base overseas. Aboriginal languages are the languages resident in Canada, born in this country. If they die out here, they will not remain anywhere in the world. Yet the Secretary of State refused to set up an institute for aboriginal languages, as proposed by one of my Liberal colleagues.
There have been continued delays and obstruction by the Minister of Indian Affairs to the settlement of important native claims and grievances. That, along with the funding cancellations, has led to the incidents we saw this summer. The refusal of the government to allow natives to be recognized, either in the constitutional process or recognized as distinct and founding peoples in
September 28, 1990

our constitution, resulted in the failure of the constitutional amendment this spring and summer.
The delays, inaction and negative actions taken against aboriginal people after the tabling of this report indicate that the government was not willing to put native people in the forefront of the agenda in this country. As a result, some significant things happened this summer.
The first was the refusal by Elijah Harper, a member of the legislature in Manitoba, to allow the constitutional amendment to pass in the Manitoba Legislative Assembly, which resulted in the failure of the constitutional amendment proposed by the government to bring Quebec into the constitutional family. That was done as a result of the refusal by the government to recognize the legitimate claims by native people in this country to be included in the Constitution and to have their society recognized as a distinctive component of Canadian society.
The second and even more damaging result in terms of what it has done to this country and it's reputation in terms of the divisions it has created between aboriginal and non-aboriginal Canadians with the government's refusal to pay attention to this agenda was the incidents we saw this summer at Kanesatake and at Kahnawake, near Montreal. The spectre of armed native warriors throwing up barricades, after years of frustration, having to resort to arms in order to persuade this government to pay attention to the aboriginal agenda, has been an embarrassment to all Canadians and an embarrassment to this country's reputation world-wide.
Those have been the results of the failure of the government to deal with the aboriginal agenda that our committee talked about and assembled in this report that was tabled in the House on March 29, 1990.
There has to be a more effective government response. There has to be a much more effective government way to deal with this aboriginal agenda.
What happened as a result of the debate on the motion that the government tabled on the first day of the House reconvening? Of course, that motion is now obsolete. Even though it is adjourned, it calls for the Mohawks and their allies to leave the treatment centre at Kanesatake, to submit to Canadian law and turn over
Routine Proceedings
their arms to the police and to the Armed Forces. That is now an obsolete motion.
It is the only thing the government has on the agenda of this House to deal with the concerns of aboriginal people. There is nothing else on the agenda in this House. Unfortunately, that is an indicator of the kind of good faith with which Canada deals with native people. There has to be something more coming from this Parliament than that feeble motion, presented the first day, which is now obsolete.
That motion also refers the issue at Kanesatake and Kahnawake to the select Standing Committee on Justice and the Solicitor General. This is a completely inappropriate reference. We should be referring that to the committee that drafted this agenda in the first place and having the confidence of native people in Canada that it is capable of dealing with those issues.
Since that motion is obsolete, I would suggest, as others have done in this House, that the government present a new motion to the House which sets up a parliamentary commission or a special inquiry into the events which led to the confrontations at Kanesatake and Kahnawake this summer, investigates the appropriateness of the behaviour of all parties involved, investigates the type of reaction that the government got involved in, and makes a report back to this House and to the people of Canada on exactly what led to that incident and provide recommendations as to how we can avoid those incidents in the future.
This is an excellent recounting of the grievances of aboriginal people in this country. I think it deserves to be read by every single member of Parliament and by all Canadians. It is basically grievances and problems as outlined by the aboriginal people of Canada themselves and conveyed to this House by the Standing Committee on Aboriginal Affairs.
Essentially what this report does is call on Parliament to make the 1990s the decade in which Canada commits itself to dealing with the aboriginal agenda. I think that some proclamation should come from the Parliament of Canada indicating that it intends to deal with the aboriginal agenda in that way, by making a proclamation declaring the 1990s to be the decade of Canada's aboriginal people, the decade in which this government and this Parliament intends to set in motion the pro-

September 28, 1990
Routine Proceedings
cesses to deal with the outstanding business that remains between Canada and its aboriginal people.
I suggest that an appropriate way to kick off this decade after a proclamation is made is to invite the native leadership of Canada to select among their number either a native leader or elder that they believe has the stature to make an address to the joint Houses of Parliament to outline to parliamentarians and to the people of Canada the hopes and aspirations of the aboriginal people of this country and what they would like to see dealt with. It has been suggested that someone of the stature of Georges Erasmus be invited to the House of Commons to present, on behalf of all aboriginal groups in Canada, a statement of the hopes and aspirations of the aboriginal people for Canada and their relations to Canada in the future.
We have had a number of heads of state address this Parliament since I have become a member of Parliament. We have had the King of Jordan address our Parliament. We have had the President of the State of Israel. However, it does not necessarily have to be restricted to a head of state. We have also had Nelson Mandela, the great African leader of the African National Congress, come to address Parliament. The one group that has yet to be recognized by Parliament in that way is the aboriginal people of this country. I think it would be appropriate to establish a decade of aboriginal people, a decade in which we commit ourselves to resolving that unfinished business, to ask the aboriginal leadership of Canada to put up one of their number, a leader or an elder, who will address the joint Houses of Parliament and outline to us their hopes and aspirations as to how they would like to participate in this country of Canada.
I think that the first thing that Parliament can do in order to demonstrate its good faith to the aboriginal people of this country, coming out of the problems that we have experienced through the last summer and in terms of the failure of the Constitutional Accord and the armed confrontations at Oka and Chateauguay, is to vote concurrence in this motion which outlines the aboriginal agenda for Canada and sets in motion a decade of activity which will complete the unfinished business between ourselves and the aboriginal people of this country.

speechtext: Questions or comments? Resuming debate. We are now, after the Minister has given the notice, back to questions and comments following the speech by the hon. member for Comox- Albemi. On a point of order, the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace.

Madam Speaker, when you called questions and comments, the hon. minister got up on a point of order with respect to Bill C-44,1 believe, and therein the confusion. Are you awaiting comments on the point of order or are we now back to the matter which was before the House?

speechtext:
Of course I am not calling questions or comments on a notice that was given by the minister on a point of order which was quite in order.
We are now returning to the 10 minute period of questions or comments following the speech by the hon. member for Comox-Albemi on concurrence in the report. No one rose on questions or comments. Is the hon. member arising on questions or comments?

Madam Speaker, I would like to ask the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Skelly), who pointed out that Mr. Erasmus should be invited to testify before this House, if he would have any objection to hearing the testimony of native chiefs or leaders from Quebec as well. I wonder because I read in this morning's papers that there is no concensus among native leaders. For instance, Mr. White Duck, from Maniwaki, criticized sharply Mr. Erasmus this morning. This cast a totally different light on the Oka crisis. Would he have a problem with Quebec native leaders testifying before us on what is happening in Quebec?
September 28, 1990

Madam Speaker, I would like to thank the member for his question. I think he misinterpreted what I suggested in terms of asking the aboriginal leaders of this country, which would include Quebec, to have one of their number address the joint Houses of Parliament. I think it would be an appropriate way of beginning a year in which this Parliament commits itself to deal with the issues, as I pointed out, that remain unfinished between Canada and its aboriginal people.
I mentioned someone of the stature of Georges Erasmus, Grand Chief of the Assembly of First Nations. No, I did not specifically ask that he be invited.
Certainly there are disagreements on issues among provinces, municipalities, political parties, and various groups. It is understandable that there would be differences among aboriginal groups as well.
I think it would be appropriate for this Parliament to call on the aboriginal leadership of this country to select one of their numbers, a chief or an elder, to come and address this Parliament on the hopes and the aspirations of the aboriginal people of this country.

Madam Speaker, I would like to know-I skimmed through the report this morning and it contains a number of statistics-whether the committee also analyses figures on housing, income and percentage of the prison population, on a province-by-province basis.
Do we have statistics by province that tell us something about housing and income and about the prison population as a percentage of the provincial figure?
I would like to know whether the committee has those statistics and if it does, could they be tabled?

Madam Speaker, what the committee was doing in its report and in the research it carried out up until March 29, 1990 which resulted in its report was trying to give Canadians a broad picture of the quality of life enjoyed by native people in Canada as compared with the quality of life enjoyed by other
Routine Proceedings
Canadians and to show that there were disparities which have to be corrected.
I know the information the hon. gentleman mentioned is available with respect to aboriginal inmates in prison on a province-by-province basis. There is a Canadian Bar Association report. There is the report of Max Yalden, Canadian Human Rights Commissioner. That information is widely available. I know there is a lower number of aboriginal people in the population of Quebec than in other provinces. However, the number of aboriginal inmates is far too high in all provinces, and that is why we have this report. It is one of the issues this report calls on Parliament to deal with.

I would like to point out, Madam Speaker, that first of all, since 1986 the Department of Indian Affairs has had information on these matters, by province, and I am somewhat surprised that they are not given here. Is it perhaps because they put Quebec in a favourable light? I am not sure.
I would also like to know why no Indians from Quebec were asked to testify before the commitee unless some were invited but did not show up. In any case, no Indians from Quebec testified before the committee. Is there any explanation for this?

Madam Speaker, I thank the questioner again. The committee makes it a practice to invite all aboriginal organizations. In this one we attempted to invite the national organizations, but others were notified and did volunteer. Included in those national organizations were organizations which do represent native people in Quebec. We felt that we had a relatively broad representation from every province in Canada and from all of the territories.
In addition, the statistics are basically national statistics because we are the national Parliament dealing with national issues. I am sure there was no intention on the part of the committee to eliminate statistics that would have been favourable to one province or another. If it has happened, it was not the committee's intention to do that.

speakeroldname: Hon. Shirley Martin (Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to rise this afternoon to discuss the committee report Unfinished Business. Certainly the committee put a

Routine Proceedings
lot of time and effort into this issue. I compliment the chairman and members of the committee, as well as those who also attended committee hearings and took part in it.
In the forward it states: "The purpose of the report is to share some of the understanding that we have accumulated". The report does not prescribe specific action other than to strongly suggest that Canadians, through their governments, have a lot of work to do in this decade. This is not a challenge facing only one government or only one minister. This is a challenge for all Canadians, a circumstance that has developed over a series of generations and one which will require concentrated commitment over many years.
I think that is an apt introduction to the report in that there is much to be done. There is also much that has been done. It is very unfortunate that the cloud of Oka this summer has obscured much of the work that has been done by the native leaders in this country and the activities they have been involved in to better the standard of living for their people and also their future.
I would like perhaps to take some of the points mentioned in the report and just review some of the things that have been happening in these particular areas.
I became Minister of State for Indian Affairs in February of this year. In the six months that I have been involved, as well as with the problems of which we are all aware, I have also had the opportunity to travel across this country to meet with many of our aboriginal people and their leaders. There are many more I would still like to have the opportunity to meet with.
One of the first things that was spoken about in the committee report was the self-government agenda of Canada. We have a program for community self-government for Indian peoples, many bands are currently looking at this as an opportunity to move forward in rightfully taking over control of the decision making for Indian people.
One of the first opportunities I had was on March 9 of this year at Whitefish Bay, Ontario, where we signed the first self-government agreement with that group. Shortly after that I had the opportunity to sign a self-government agreement at New Credit, Ontario. It was rather a unique self-government agreement in that it was done with the Mississaugas and Chippawas of Ontario and it is
a two-level self-government agreement. The band council itself will take on certain responsibilities, and the nine band councils and chiefs will take on other responsibilities.
These two particular signings gave me the opportunity to see from our native people the need to make sure that the programs that we have are flexible, because what met the self-government needs at Whitefish Bay would not have met, if it had been a standard self-government agreement, the needs for the people of the Mississaugas and the Chippawas at New Credit. It is very important that we keep flexibility within self-government agreements.
As mentioned earlier, many bands are looking at it. We have agreements that are close to signing and others where bands are now exploring. The whole purpose of it is that the bands themselves must first want to enter into the agreement. They must have an idea of what they want, the type of self-government that they want. Then we will sit down and work along with them to bring about an agreement that meets their needs within the framework of Canada's Constitution.
Land claims is another issue about which there has been much discussion in the debates this week. On August 23 of this year I met with the Indian Chiefs of Ontario, the Indian Commissioner of Ontario, and members of the provincial government. We sat at that meeting and one of the important requests that came out of it was a request put to Mr. Harry Laforme, the Indian Commissioner of Ontario, to bring about a report on land claim process: what was wrong with it, why it was not working, and recommendations for change.
Mr. Laforme has done done an excellent job. In fact his report was just tabled this morning. Here we are a month and a few days from that initial request to put the report together, and he has done it. I look forward to reviewing the report, when I have an opportunity to do so, and seeing what we can do to take his recommendations and put some of them into operation. He negotiated or discussed input with chiefs across Canada. Much of it came from his own experience in negotiating land claims in Ontario. I am really looking forward to working on the results of the report and seeing what can be done to implement it. Certainly we send our congrat-
September 28, 1990

ulations to Mr. Laforme for presenting so quickly the report that we can start to work on.
I am sure my counterpart, when he is named in the provincial government in the coming week, and I will be able to get together and work. The provinces across this country have a large responsibility when it comes to land claims and it is something that we have to work together on.
The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development has been working with the people of Saskatchewan and of British Columbia on land claim issues there as well. We have some indications of agreement from the premier of British Columbia that he too is willing to work toward settling land claims in British Columbia.
Things have been happening on this matter. We are certainly going to continue to work in this area, with the help and the contribution of native peoples across Canada.
We hope to sign and work on land claims in the future. Certainly much has been done in the way of land claims since this government took office in 1984. We have signed agreements to settle claims both of a comprehensive type and of a specific claim type. I have been part of some of those in Ontario. Certainly my hon. colleague, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, has also signed them in the north.
We are proud of those agreements. They are agreements that have been a long time coming. The process is too slow and something has to be done to speed them up, but certainly we have signed and entered into negotiation on more land claims since this government took office than was done for many years prior.
As we go through the report, we see another point that was touched on by the committee. It was the need for economic development as a very important tool for the future development and progress of our native people.
The CAEDS program that our government put into operation is starting to work very well for native people. I have had the opportunity to work with several Indian bands on their programs. They have some very interest-
Routine Proceedings
ing and innovative ideas for changes in economic development. We have committed some $1.4 billion to native economic development over the next five-year period. There are some very interesting projects coming forward. We have a board whereby native people themselves make decisions as to whether or not a business should be funded.
We have a real responsibility to make sure as we help native people develop in the business field that they are successful and have all the backing that they require. Native businesses started some 20 years ago and we now have 5,000 native businesses. Some 2,500 of those have been developed within the last six months.
Our native people are making great strides in economic development, but as I mentioned earlier there is still more that can be done.
On the environment issues, I do not think there is a people in this country who has a better understanding or lives more closely to the land than our aboriginal people.
The Minister of the Environment worked on the development of The Green Plan which included an environmental strategy. The northern part of Canada must be protected.
We held consultative hearings The Green Plan which I attended in Yellowknife and Iqaluit. I had an opportunity to hear first hand the input from the native people and the concerns they had about conservation of resources, about protection of the water, and about the protection of the landscape itself. Much in the way of material has been left behind in the Arctic that must be removed and shipped out. It will be expensive, but it is required. When it comes to the Arctic environment, it is something that we cannot do alone in Canada because the Arctic is not exclusively ours. We are working internationally with other countries to ensure that we can work toward a clean environment in the Arctic.
We have consulted with our aboriginal people in the northern part of the country and will continue to do so. There are sections within the land claim agreements which offer the opportunity to put together groups so that native people will have a say in what is done as far as

September 28, 1990
Routine Proceedings
environment and economic issues are concerned within their area.
Another point that I would like to touch on in the report is education. Education is a key to the future for our aboriginal people, but there is one underlying theme in education that must be followed. The very proud heritage and culture of aboriginal people must be maintained in the education of the future.
On Wednesday I came back from Fort Hope, Ontario where I had the honour of opening a new school in that community. It is a beautiful building, one that has been designed to fit in with the landscape and nature. It is of wood with many glass windows so that the students do not feel confined. As we were opening the building, the chief made the very important point that when it comes to schools and education the building is only a shell, that it is really only what happens within that building that is important as far as education is concerned.
They have classes in that school on native culture and native language which are taught by the elders. This is their link to the past and their preservation for the future. They are also equipped with computers whereby they can provide the children of Port Hope the opportunity to be prepared for the future and to be able to progress as the country and the world are progressing in technology and in knowledge, but at the same time not forget where they come from and their veiy proud heritage.
I was also in Norway House in Manitoba where they have done a great deal of work on education for students who had dropped out of school and want to return and for elders who want to improve their knowledge and their skills. They have a very interesting computer program. The first thing the program does is to test the reading level of the individual. It looks at the course individuals want to take and then it adjusts that course to their reading levels so that if they need help with their reading skills they are not held back from completing the course they may want. At the same time it produces a course to increase their reading skills.
This is the type of change in education that is necessary. It is more than just the three r's that are necessary. We have to be able to identify the needs, produce the programs to answer those needs, and ensure that the
resources and facilities are there in order for it to happen.
We do not have enough of these types of schools. It is something we are committed to work on both at the curriculum level and the physical level. Another thing that is necessary is the opportunity for native people to be involved in the administration of education. They need to be in a position to enter into decisions on curriculum and school facilities. In some cases, this could be through a school board, which is an area that is being looked at.
I was in Fort Francis where the native representative on the local school board has been elected chairman of that board and is having a real influence as far as native education is concerned.
Even before the children get to school there is a need for child care. Many of our native mothers who have not been able to better themselves through education because of having the responsibility of motherhood, are entering training courses and child care is very necessary for them.
In June, I met with a group in Meadow Lake who, through the Minister of National Health and Welfare's innovation program for child care, have begun a program that I was very pleased to hear about. It was one of the recommendations that we made in the special committee on child care, which I had the privilege to chair in 1985.
They have entered into what in the committee we called a "hub and spoke" situation whereby there is centralized control and supervision of child care which is conducted in homes throughout the reserves. They have brought together more than one reserve, so that the core supervisory and administrative needs are met by a small group, but is far-reaching. There are native homes for the children to attend throughout the reserves in the area where they can still stay within their native culture. The administration of that care can be done with native supervision in a centralized office.
I am looking forward to watching that program grow. I think it is an ideal example of how child care can be handled where you do not have large needs, as in a metro area, but rather small needs over a much wider area.

So we are moving in those areas, and as I mentioned earlier, will continue to do so. Unfortunately, I will probably have to continue to say for several years that things are going to be moving more slowly than what we would like, but they are moving.
I think the statement by the Prime Minister in the House this week where he outlined the four pillars of future relationships with aboriginal people, the work that has to be done in the land claims area to speed that up and also in the whole relationship between governments and native people was a very important. I think that goes a long way to really cement the work that has been started. He has given his full commitment to it and I know he will continue to support the efforts and, in fact, continue to direct us to ensure that those commitments are met in the future and are met as quickly as possible.
I appreciate the opportunity to speak to this report and to again compliment the committee on the work that it has done. I look forward to the work that it will continue to do as a very important committee in the structure of the House of Commons.

Madam Speaker, while I am encouraged by the positive tone of the Minister of State's presentation, I am a little concerned about the recent fiscal arrangements of the junior minister. I point out that a document dated March 15, 1990, put together by the Assembly of First Nations analysed the last budget put forward by the government, and tell us a few outstanding facts. The two-year fiscal reduction of $100 million is deceptively buried in the 1991 main estimates of the budget papers, $26 million was cut from approved levels for capital facilities and community services, $15 million from band management, $7 million from welfare services and $2 million from economic development for each of the two years.
The question I have for the junior minister is this. With a crippled economic base and no tax base, just where do native people find the finances to offset lost federal revenues?
Can the Minister of State explain to us if she is prepared to readjust the glaring inadequacies of the last budget and actually turn around that funding to Canada's first people?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as the hon. member for Hamilton West mentioned, the reductions he spoke
Routine Proceedings
about was in the proposed budget. When you look at the budget of last year compared to this year, the increase in funding in the budget of Indian Affairs was actually 8 per cent. Our budget was raised, compared to other budgets within the government. While they were all taking cuts from actuals, we were taking a reduction in what we had hoped to spend. But our budget still increased 8 per cent over the budget from the previous year.
For instance, the increases in education were some 8.7 per cent, for a total budget of $736 million; the economic development increases were 28.4 per cent, an increase of $20.5 million; under land revenues and trust we had an increase of $11 million, which was 23.8 per cent, for a total budget of $58 million. The government also invested an additional $28 million into on-reserve capital facilities and related services.
The other thing that also should be taken under consideration, is that under the current financial arrangements, we have entered into what we call alternate funding arrangements. Alternate funding arrangements provide for the administration of funds by the Indian bands themselves and not by the Government of Canada. This is the way it should be.
Seventy-two per cent of the Indian and Inuit fair budget is administered by the bands, not by the Government of Canada. They must report to us on an annual basis with an audit. But we no longer do, as the party to which this member belongs used to do in a very paternalistic way, decide how the money should be spent, not the Indian people. We have moved to that. We have increased the budget. Not only have we increased the budget, but we have given control of that budget where it belongs, the Indian people themselves. They decide within their capital budget what they want to spend it on. They decide within their operating budget what they want to spend it on, and they are doing well with it.
No, we did not get as much in the 1990 budget as we would have liked, but we did get an increase over 1989 and we have worked with that increase to make sure those dollars are well spent and spent under the control of the native people of this countiy. The AFAs are working very, very well.
Again I have had the privilege of signing about four or five of these since March of this year. There are many other bands who want to enter into this arrangement and when they have reached the stage where they feel they

Routine Proceedings
are in a position to take over the control of the spending, then that control will be given to them.
This is another reason why education is so important. We need more young Indian people taking business and economic courses so they can use the funds provided to them to make a better future for the Indian community.
Yes, there were reductions from what we had hoped we would get, but we still had an 8 per cent increase. I think that increase has been spent wisely because it is under the control of the Indian people.
of the comments that he made and make sure that they are passed on to my colleague as well.
The point that I was attempting to make concerning the CAEDS budget was that the native people have a role to play in assessing the value of the projects that come forward. The final authority still lies, in some cases, within the minister's office, but not in all cases. It depends upon the size of the requirement for a particular project that comes forward. The fact is that we are involving the native people in the decision making. I think we have to look through the whole program.

Madam Speaker, I have a couple of questions I would like to ask the minister.
It is all very interesting to hear what the government is saying today in terms of what more they can do for the aboriginal people. I think one of the best examples of what they can do to ensure that the aboriginal people are going to trust this government is make a couple of changes in their land claims policy.
First, it should adopt a policy that the aboriginal people have the inherent right to self-government and; second, take out the extinguishment clause in the land claims policy. Those are the two issues I would suggest that the minister talk to her colleagues to see what they can do to adopt them.
The minister made reference to the Canadian Aboriginal Economic Development Strategy, which by the way was started under the leadership of the Liberal party as the Native Economic Development Program. The minister mentioned that it was the aboriginal people who make the decisions on whether or not to award funding or loans to aboriginal groups. Does not the final approval rest with the minister at this time?
It is not the huge corporations that we often think of, or very large programs and businesses. There are a lot of small businesses that, given the opportunity to start under the CAEDS program, can grow to something very large. More than that, it is not only a business opportunity for the individual who wants to start it but it is a business opportunity on reserve, or off reserve, but basically on reserve, to offer jobs to native people. It offers a service to native people that they often do not have. It is those small and very important businesses that we must address and make sure that they are funded so that they can give the individual the economic opportunity, the job opportunities for native people on reserve and the services that are necessary within that area.

Madam Speaker, the last couple of days and months have been important. Watching the television just yesterday morning where it showed that picture of personnel from the army with an Indian women with her child in her arms reminded me of visiting Cyprus. I thought that we would never have to resort to such a thing here in Canada. Yet, we saw those pictures for almost 70 days.
The hon. minister got up and gave us an overview of education. She also spoke of the environment in the Arctic and what the government, with other countries, is doing. I would like to challenge the hon. minister to name those countries.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in answer to the first question that the hon. member raises, the whole issue of land claims, both comprehensive and specific, are being looked at in the department, along with consultation with the native people of this country, to see what can be done to make them more effective. I will take cognizance
My most important question for which I have not yet received an answer is why this government and this minister did not go to her boss, the Prime Minister of this country, and ask him to recall the Parliament last summer?


We can sit here for the whole day but my questions are precise. Why did they not recall Parliament? Would the hon. minister tell me what other countries that they are dealing with on the environment in the Arctic?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Government of Canada, along with seven other countries in the circumpolar area, has formed a group which has already held meetings and which has been working on the Arctic environment. I hope my memory serves me correctly on the countries that are involved. They are the U.S.S.R., Norway, Finland and Greenland. They come to mind initially. I think what the hon. member must realize is that the water that flows into the Arctic comes from our Mackenzie Valley river system. We have very, very little industry within that particular area. But also flowing into that same body of water that provides the water in the north for our native people are river systems coming from deep within the U.S.S.R. where it is highly industrialized. We do not know what the sources of the contaminants are, we do not know if it is coming from a river system within the U.S.S.R. or whether it is coming from our own Mackenzie Valley.
We cannot clean the Arctic up on our own. We can only clean the Arctic up with the co-operation of the other countries in the area. That is why we have been, very, very active within the circumpolar group. Meetings have been held and we will still continue to hold meetings. We have had representatives in the U.S.S.R. who have been working with people there. It is a very serious matter and we feel that by working together with all of the countries in the circumpolar group we will be able to make a difference in the Arctic, differences that are very, very necessary.

Madam Speaker, what the aboriginal people of this country feel about the recent events and the way the government has been acting, I would say, to paraphrase a former Prime Minister of this country, welcome to the 1990s. I say that because I think that whatever happens over the next few years, never again will our concerns and issues be put on the backburner.
The Prime Minister has been saying that we are going to have a new agenda for the aboriginal people. Yesterday The Globe and Mail, after the pull out at Oka, stated "that Prime Minister Brian Mulroney praised the army and stressed that the government had not made any
Routine Proceedings
concessions." The rule of law has prevailed so the Prime Minister was all praise for the army.
I must admit that throughout the Oka situation, there have not been any shots fired at anybody. However, in saying that there had been no violence, I would just like to point out that we saw, live on TV and in the newspapers, as pictures, of a woman and her daughter being thrown to the ground by the army. So when people say there was no violence, one can be very selective about the description of violence. We saw tanks, machine guns, helicopters hovering overhead at night, we saw a razor wire-I am not exactly sure what a razor wire does but I suspect it is not that easy to just cross over a razor wire-we saw communications cut off from the rest of the world to the group and we saw all sorts of intimidation tactics. So I do not think that we can all rest easy that there were no further deaths after the unfortunate death of Corporal Lemay.
I do not think we can all rest easy and say, "it is over". We can all say, "Thank God, it is over", but we cannot just shove it off to the backburner and say, "Well, nobody died". There was violence. Unfinished business, I think, is really an apt description for the report. I think we will over the years attempt to do justice to this report. I think it is perfect timing for this report. Hopefully the government will be announcing major new initiatives. So far it has not announced concrete initiatives. All we have been hearing are words, nice words, but only words to date.
As I mentioned earlier in my question, I would like to touch on the subject of land claims. Again I hesitate to use the words "land claims". What are we doing? We are trying to claim some land from the government, land that was never given up, land that was never ceded, land that was never surrendered to any government, to anybody, except in a few cases down south. When I say never I mean the eastern Arctic, the area that I represent, more than anywhere else. But there are a lot of cases around here as well.
That is why I think until such time as the government recognizes our problem with the issue of extinguishment of aboriginal rights, there will be other forms of protest against the government continuing over the years until such time as the government recognizes that there is a need to recognize that inherent right to self-government. Until there is that recognition, we cannot just give up rights which we have never given up and which in

September 28, 1990
Routine Proceedings
some cases supersede the Constitution and the laws of Canada, as has been pointed out by various court cases.
One of the great errors or misconceptions by the Canadian people is that when people think of aboriginal issues or aboriginal people, they think in terms of social problems and issues only. I think that people have to be aware that we want participation in economic situations, the constitutional development and the political arena, not just on social issues.
Aboriginal people are more than social problems. It is time that people realized that they cannot continue to treat it as a social problem only, but must start treating aboriginal issues as ones that need to be addressed at all levels and forms.
The Prime Minister stated yesterday or the day before that one of the first things they were going to do was do away with the issue of six land claims at a time. This I think bodes well for the numerous land claims negotiations that are going on. However, these could have been addressed long before this. Why has it taken this government six years to address this issue? Why has it taken that long to address the issue?
Approximately a year and a half ago, in April 1989, the government delivered a Throne Speech, mentioning the words "aboriginal" or "the north"' three times in that very short speech. I said: "It sounds like they are sort of giving us"-I cannot remember the proper term, I think it was something like "the velvet glove; you make sure that they notice that they have been mentioned three times but what we do afterward is not necessarily what we say we are going to do". That is exactly what has happened over the past year. There has been nothing done. Probably as much as aboriginal groups do not condone the armed conflict, there probably would not have been anything done if it had not been for the events at Kanesatake and Oka.
I think that as a result of what happened also in June there would have been a lot less done until aboriginal issues made the issue of the day through various media forums. It was very heartening to see how strong the power of a word can be when watching for something like a week or maybe a little longer a member of the legislature in Manitoba say "no", and that is all he said. It was very, very interesting to see that. It quite put in the
perspective of what the power of a word can do when a person is determined to do something.
I mentioned earlier that all the nice words that are being said now have to be followed up. When Elijah Harper said "no" to the Speaker, he meant to follow through. That is exactly what we are saying to the government. When you are saying whatever you are going to be doing for the aboriginal people, you have to be able to follow through over the course of the next number of years.
It is very urgent that the government of the day also recognize that we cannot let what happened over the summer to just be forgotten. The government has to allow an independent inquiry into the events at Oka, a special independent inquiry to ensure that everything comes out, how all the things about came about or what happened.
I was talking about the violence that we saw. I am not even sure that what we saw. I am not at all sure whether there was more. What happened when the cameras were not around at Oka? What happened that the cameras did not see? We do not know. When you see violence, you think of physical violence only. I remember over the course of the summer where food was not allowed to go through, where people were not allowed to go through, all sorts of things. It was a basic abuse of human rights. Therefore, there has to be full inquiry into that issue. The Canadian people have to know what really happened.
On the first day after the session of Parliament started, the government put a motion forward praising the actions of the army. It was quite unbelievable that the government would do that when the issue was still going on. How could it have foreseen what was going to happen?
Now that the issue is over would have been the proper time to put forward a motion. Again, the motion did not address the real issue.
The government through this motion is really trying to gain political points. At the same time, it is trying to make sure that the opposition party might vote against its motion so that it can say to the the Canadian people
September 28, 1990

that the opposition voted against a motherhood issue. It is a motherhood issue.
We all know the army was doing its job. We do not argue with that, but to try to separate what the army was doing to the people at Oka and what the army as a whole is supposed to do is not what we would have agreed with. Instead of being non-partisan about the whole issue at Oka, the government decided to be partisan and tried to make the opposition look bad through its motion.
The constitutional issue of recognition of aboriginal people as a distinct group of people has to be recognized by the government and by the Canadian people as a whole. The Prime Minister keeps saying that the constitutional talks failed. What he selectively forgets is that the 1983 Constitutional Conference chaired by the previous Prime Minister of Canada, Pierre Trudeau, was successful in that it got some amendments that were proclaimed in June 1984.
Again, Quebec did not sign the Accord, but nine other provinces did. So there were some constitutional amendments made in their respective legislatures. There was some success at the Constitutional Conferences.
It was the last two that had no hope of success. In one instance in the last Constitutional Conference, the Prime Minister walked out without even the benefit of trying to come to an agreement. This is basically saying that it was not important enough to try to get the agreement of all the provinces.
Shortly after, the Prime Minister basically locked up 10 premiers until they got an agreement together and came out with a flawed constitutional amendment. Fortunately for the aboriginal people of this country, it was killed by an aboriginal person in the legislature of Manitoba.
One of the areas that the minister touched on was the economic conditions, the Canadian Aboriginal Economic Development Strategy. One of the problems that I as a previous member of the Native Accounting Development Program encountered was that we always had a lack of capital for the aboriginal people, a lack of equity.
There were always various businesses wanting to start up, but because of a he lack of equity, they could not do it. It is all very well for the government to say it is going out with the Canadian Aboriginal Economic Develop-
Routine Proceedings
ment Strategy. However, if it is not prepared to give special consideration to the aboriginal peoples' conditions or financial state, that may fail. I hope the department will take that into account, the fact that there is a lack of equity among the aboriginal people and until such time that that is taken into account by groups like the Canadian Aboriginal Economic Development Strategy, we will not have a chance.

Madam Speaker, in the report Unfinished Business which we are discussing this afternoon, there are some very interesting statistics at the back of the report in Appendix C which is entitled "Socio-economic Conditions of Native People in Canada". If one looks at those statistics, one notes that in many areas the situation is much worse for Inuit people than it is for Indians. Of course, for both aboriginal groups it is very bad compared to other Canadians. For example, with respect to life expectancy, the life expectancy of a Canadian male is 72 years of age and for a female it is 79 years of age but for Inuit, it is 60 years in Labrador, 62 years in northern Quebec and 66 years in the Northwest Territories, much below that of the Canadian non-Inuit person.
If one looks at infant mortality for all Canadians, it is eight deaths per 1,000 births but for Inuit it is 28 deaths per 1,000 births. This is a horrible record. When one looks at suicide statistics for Canadians, there are 15 suicides per 100,000 people and for status Indians there are 34 suicides per 100,000 status Indians, but for Inuit in the Northwest Territories there are 54 suicides per
100.000	Inuit. The incidence of violent death is 54 per
100.000	Canadians and for Inuit there are 173 violent deaths per 100,000 people. In the area of overcrowded housing, only 2 per cent of non-aboriginal people live in overcrowded housing, whereas 31 per cent of the Inuit live in overcrowded housing. Only 17 per cent of nonaboriginal Canadians did not attend high school but for Inuit, 53 per cent have not attended high school and for status Indians it is 45 per cent.
We listened at an attempt at justification by the minister a few minutes ago of what was being done for aboriginal people. I would like the hon. member for Nunatsiaq, himself an Inuit, to tell this House, faced with these statistics whether his people can take seriously the statement made by the minister.

September 28, 1990
Routine Proceedings

I seem to have a lot of work to do and I have only got 26 years left of my life expectancy. I thank the hon. member for his question.
It is very true what the hon. member was pointing out in terms of housing, benefits to the Inuit and in terms of health. I take a special case in the Keewatin region area where I am from. All our patients are taken to Churchill or Winnipeg. That in itself may not seem so bad, but just imagine a woman who is having a baby having to go to Churchill or Winnipeg, cities in a different province, for a month and if it is a special case, maybe up to two months. That in itself may not seem so bad, but it is the psychological effects that it has on the family. That creates stress, and those kinds of things are prevailing.
Yes, there is very poor housing. We used to try to point out to the Government of the Northwest Territories the difference between the houses which the government provided for its employees and the low cost or low rental houses the government provided for-and I do not say just Inuit-the people, as well as the amount of money that was poured into the houses for civil servants and the amount of money that was not poured into the regular houses.
In terms of other issues, we have the highest suicide rate. I just want to point out that I have lost two brothers to suicide. That kind of thing is very much a case. It is time that we hold the government to the words it is using, that we take the government to task.

Madam Speaker, the hon. member for Nunatsiaq told us that he felt insulted when the government presented a motion stating that it praised the army for its conduct during the events at Oka.
I would like to say that we in the Bloc Quebecois also spoke out against the first paragraph of the motion, but I must say I am surprised that the Liberal Party, of which he is a member, did not challenge this passage in its amendment. I suppose it agreed, at the time.
In any case, I would like to ask him-he must be knowledgeable about aboriginal land claims-how many agreements have been signed so far and in which provinces?

I must admit some ignorance here, Madam Speaker, as much as I hate to do it. Very few land claims agreements have been signed. Although hundreds of land claims have been put forward by aboriginal groups across the country, to date there have been very few settlements of cases.

Madam Speaker, I would like to say there have been four agreements to date, three of which were concluded in Quebec and a fourth in the Yukon, but only Quebec, as a province, is taking part in negotiations, since all other provinces have so far refused to do so.

Madam Speaker, I do not think we have any lessons to learn from the member. As a member from the Northwest Territories let me say that we have one land claim negotiated under the Inuvialuit. We have two claims under process already. The Government of the Northwest Territories takes part in all discussions with respect to the ongoing land claims negotiations with the federal government. The province of Quebec is not an exception.

Madam Speaker, I want to take the time to congratulate my hon. colleague for the work that he is doing in this particular field and for the time he spent over the last two to three months dealing with the way his people were being treated.
I want to put to him the question that I tried to put to the minister and unfortunately got no answer, due to the fact that maybe the minister danced around or ran out of time. Does the hon. member think that this government should have recalled Parliament right away when the Oka crisis broke, yes or no?

Madam Speaker, very shortly after this happened on July 11, the Liberal Party of Canada asked for a recall of Parliament, remembering that two years previously the government had recalled Parliament because of 117 boat people coming into one of the maritime provinces.
I think that Parliament should have been recalled. The issue would have been dealt with much faster. Shortly after Parliament returned there was a disengagement of
September 28, 1990

the incident in Oka. The events of the whole summer could have been prevented if the Government of Canada had recalled Parliament.

speakeroldname: Hon. Mary Collins (Associate Minister of National Defence and Minister responsible for Status of Women):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise today to participate in this debate on the report of the Standing Committee on Aboriginal Affairs entitled Unfinished Business.
I very much enjoyed this report. I recall in 1984, just after I first came to Parliament, that I served on that standing committee. I know the good work that was done during that time when Mr. Penner was involved with that committee. I am very pleased that good work is continuing that good work under the chair of the hon. member for Macleod.
There is just one paragraph in the report that deals with aboriginal women. The committee indicates that the Native Women's Association was unable to appear during the set of hearings that led up to this report, but it indicates that it is aware of some of the issues aboriginal women would wish to discuss. Certainly in other areas of the report it talked about child care, housing, and education, issues which I know the Aboriginal Women's Association would have brought to the committee's attention.
I would like to discuss some of those issues, some of the government's response, and some of our initiatives to deal with those issues.
However, before I move on to that, Mr. Speaker, I would just like to comment on a remark made a bit earlier by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni who opened this debate. He indicated that he felt that other than the motion which was put on the floor and debated on Tuesday of this week, there really had not been anything substantive or specific about what this government's actions were with respect to aboriginal people in this country.
I would beg to disagree. This week in almost every Question Period I think there have been questions raised on issues arising either specifically out of the situation at Oka and Kahnawake or broader issues about Indian land claims and self-government. The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and other ministers who have responded have indicated their specific plans to proceed in a rapid and appropriate way to start to deal effectively with some of these issues. This was all
Routine Proceedings
predicated upon the peaceful resolution of the situation at Oka, one that we were pleased to see occur on Wednesday of this week.
The most important contribution to this over-all debate-and I am sure it is a contribution which in the minds of many Canadians has been vitally important in helping them think about these difficult issues-was a speech made by the Prime Minister on Tbesday, September 25. I remind members that the Prime Minister on that occasion did indeed set out a very specific agenda. He said:
The agenda I believe we ought to be addressing will have four main pillars: land claims, the economic and social conditions on reserves, the relationship between aboriginal peoples and governments, and concerns of Canada's aboriginal peoples in contemporary Canadian life.
He then went on and quite specifically talked about three initiatives in areas of land claims. Certainly the one that I am very pleased about, being a member from British Columbia, is that we will be abandoning the old style of only being able to deal with six land claims at a time. The largest number of outstanding land claims are in my province of British Columbia, and it has been very difficult to move ahead with them under the constraints of the old policy. I welcome the announcement and congratulate the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and the Prime Minister on it. That, along with the provinces' indication that they will be prepared to undertake joint discussions, I hope will mean that we will be able to move ahead substantially with land claims issues in British Columbia.
The other dimension that the Prime Minister talked about related to social conditions on reserves. All members who have had the opportunity of visiting reserves across this country know the variety of conditions. There are some that are excellent. I have in my own riding the Mount Currie community where the previous government and this government together provided the funds to establish basically a whole new community with very good housing and support services.
However, we know that is not the case in some parts of the country like northern Ontario. The Prime Minister's commitment that we were going to be working with the Indian leadership and the provincial governments on a range of improvements to basic community programs

September 28, 1990
Routine Proceedings
and services such as water and sewage facilities will be welcomed by our native people across this country.
It is something that is fundamentally needed in order to move on to some of the other kinds of programs that are so essential, but I think the point the Prime Minister made as well is something we should all reflect on when we talk about the essential of ensuring that our native people have a sense of dignity. Of course that sense of dignity can only come as their own self-esteem is developed and grown, and perhaps in no area more importantly than for aboriginal women. Of all the issues we talk about and the difficulties we face with respect to aboriginal people, aboriginal women are often and frequently more disadvantaged than perhaps others.
When I came to Parliament, the very first piece of legislation I was involved in-and I sat on the committee-was Bill C-31, a bill that this government brought forward to redress a basic inequality which many aboriginal women in this country had faced for decades and decades: the fact that if an aboriginal woman married a non-aboriginal male she was disenfranchised; she no longer had status and her children no longer had status. I think the hon. member who is sitting in the chair right now served on that committee with me.
Not aboriginal. Only Indian.

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Indian, I am sorry. He and the hon. member opposite will recall the many hearings we went through and the delegations that came to appear before that committee. There were diverse opinions. It was not something where there was unanimity.
However, this government had made the commitment and that legislation became law in June, 1985.1 think we all recall Flora MacDonald, a previous colleague of ours, who provided a lot of leadership on this issue during the 1980s.
That bill has made a difference, that change in legislation. It has meant that Indian women who were disenfranchised have been able to come back to their bands and obtain membership and housing. However, we know that the implementation has not been universally equitable across this county. Indeed there are some difficulties with that.
One of the provisions was that this piece of legislation would come up for a five-year review. I must say that those colleagues of mine who served on that committee, and others, where these kinds of provisions were included were seeing how important they are and that automatic review of legislation after a period of time by parliamentary committees is very important, because we cannot know everything when we write these laws. Sometimes they work out a little differently. They certainly may need some changes or amendments.
Over the last five years, in order to implement this legislation the government has committed some $859 million. Those funds have gone to bands. In this current year, 1990-1991, there will be about $17 million in funds for secondary and elementary education. There will be another $37 million for post-secondary education. There has been funds for housing and funds to support the reinstatement of these Indian women.
In the past little while a special committee has been established. I think it is an indication of the kind of collaboration and consultation to which this government and this Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development is committed. The committee is chaired by Bill Monsieur, Chief of the Six Nations Reserves, and includes memberships from the AFM, from the Native Women's Association of Canada, and from the Saskatchewan Federation of Indian Nations.
We expect that the committee will make its report around the end of November and will be making recommendations for improvements in the legislation to deal with some of the difficulties that are still faced. I am certainly looking forward to that report and to improvements to ensure that Indian women do have true equality.
Another area that I think is very important-and my colleague, the Minister of State for Indian Affairs and Northern Development, mentioned it as well-is economic development programs which will enable native people to take control over their own destinies and their own economic activities. The CAEDS program was mentioned already, the Canadian Aboriginal Economic Development Strategy which is under the jurisdiction of my colleague, the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism. It has been an important component.
September 28, 1990

We are already seeing that some $875 million has been designated under that program for the first five years. Also that program emphasizes partnerships with non-government groups as a primary vehicle for native economic self-sufficiency.
In my own agency of the Status of Women we have been working with our provincial colleague. At our federal-provincial meetings of ministers we put forward a plan of action for aboriginal women's economic development. In collaboration and co-operation with three national native women's organizations-the Native Women's Association of Canada, the Inuit Women's Association and the Indian and Inuit Nurses of Canada-we have undertaken a strategy and a plan to provide greater opportunities for aboriginal women to have access to funds through CAEDS and other government programs to advance economic development.
We are all aware that in Canada it is women who are starting up small businesses. I think it is something like two or three times as frequently as men and they are twice as successful. That the same pattern exists within the aboriginal community. I know my colleague from Nunatsiaq would agree with that. I know from my own riding where I have three Indian reserves just how effective some of the Indian women have been in their small businesses, but they do need support, capital, and opportunities. I am looking forward, as I am working with my colleagues, to the implementation of an aboriginal women's economic development plan and that being done in consultation.
All these programs have to be done with native people. They have to set out what they think will work. Governments, bureaucrats, and politicians do not know necessarily what is right. These programs have to be done as partnerships.
The time is getting short, but I just want to mention three other important issues that relate to aboriginal women. We all know the importance of child are. It was raised earlier today in Question Period. Certainly for native families it is very important. Through the child care initiatives fund, we have had 53 projects to support native families. That includes both on and off reserve at $5.7 million. Certainly that is a good start. The Minister of State for Indian Affairs and Northern Development has visited some of those projects, as I hope to do in the next little while as well.
Routine Proceedings
Project Haven, which is an initiative of this government under our Family Violence Program, provides support for capital for the construction of shelters for women who have been abused. Under that program, 87 spaces have been provided for native women and their children.
As well, the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development has a special $3 million allocated under the Family Violence Program for its initiatives. I know when I have talked to my ministerial colleagues from the Northwest Territories, Minister Marie-Jewell and Minister Margaret Joe from the Yukon who are native women themselves, one of the issues that is really the top concerns is this issue of violence against women within aboriginal communities. We are looking forward to working together on new programs to support and to try to not only provide assistance to women who are victims of abuse, but to try more vigorously to look at the root causes and work on prevention and education programs to hopefully some day eradicate this issue. I know my time is up-

On behalf of my party we are prepared to stay here for the

entire weekend, if necessary, to deal with this important matter.

If it is an hour, I will certainly agree to that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I really apologize for members of the House when they try to work in political manoeuvring.
We all know that we adjourn the House at three o'clock. This is to allow members of Parliament to return to their ridings when they have duties for the weekend.
