maintopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   CRIMINAL CODE MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
that Bill C-207, an act to amend the Criminal Code (hate propaganda-age group) be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Madam Speaker, I am pleased to rise this afternoon to bring to the attention of this House a matter which should be of concern to all of us in Canada. I am speaking of the violence against children; more particularly, I am speaking of the issue of the hate propaganda against children which I believe to be a cause of this violence.
There exists a product in this country today which is known as Garbage Pail Kids. This product exists in our country, but luckily, I suppose, it is not manufactured in our country. It is produced elsewhere and brought across the border into Canada. This product, which I referred to previously as Garbage Pail Kids, is produced in the form of a bubble gum card. These bubble gum cards depict
Private Members' Business
children being mutilated, murdered and dissected. The whole purpose of this is supposed to be to provide entertainment, and I use that word very loosely. The product in question is designed to be sold to children. The cards in question are sold with bubble gum, therefore the purchaser is intended to be a child. The child purchasing this sees other children in positions that I have described earlier and as such, the whole exercise cheapens the value of human life in ways that are almost too sad to describe.
I will take but a moment and give you a quick description of these cards. There is a picture of a child whose back is being scratched and where you see blood flying everywhere. This child is being scratched with a rake and the joke is supposed to be, rake Jake. That is supposed to be the name of the child in question.
In another one of those so-called funny cards, we have a child whose name is Mason Mace and he is being clubbed over the head with a spiked mace and his head is falling off. All of this, of course, is supposed to be funny, accordingly to, at least, the promoters of these products. The Topps Bubble Gum company was interviewed when I brought this to the attention of Canadians some three years ago. When they were interviewed, they said children liked gross and these cards are gross. That may be so, Madam Speaker, I do not think there is anyone who will disagree with the fact that they are gross, but that does not make them right.
I have complained about these cards on several occasions. I wrote a letter in August of 1988 to the senior assistant Crown attorney of Ottawa, the judicial district of Ottawa-Carleton, who, of course, is an employee of the Ministry of the Attorney General of Ontario, to see whether these cards offended the provisions of the Criminal Code. He wrote back to me at that time and indicated that although the cards were certainly not acceptable beyond any stretch of the imagination, that there was nothing that he could do because of the way the Criminal Code is written. I wrote further to the then Minister of National Revenue, the member for Central Nova, bringing the matter to his attention as well, describing how these cards were offensive and objectionable and why they should not be permitted to come into this country from the United States.

Private Members' Business
On September 20, 1988, the minister wrote to me and said that he had had his officials review the schedules of the Customs Tariff Act which prohibit the importation into Canada of certain material. The minister says in his letter and I am paraphrasing here, that he does find the material offensive and objectionable, however, it is not permitted by him to stop the importation of these awful cards into Canada because they do not offend the hate propaganda provisions of the Criminal Code of Canada.
Madam Speaker, the Criminal Code of Canada, under its hate propaganda provision states: "Everyone who advocates or promotes genocide is guilty of an indictable offence and liable for imprisonment of not longer than five years." It says further that: "In this section genocide means any of the following acts committed against an identifiable group." The identifiable group is further defined by saying the following: "In this section, identifiable group means any section of the public distinguished by colour, race, religion or ethnic origin." Of course, children are of all races of ethnic origin, colour and race, therefore, because these cards do not promote hatred against a specific origin, religion or race of children, the minister was apparently unable to stop the importation into Canada of this awful material. What I propose to do in my private members' bill is very simple. I propose to add one word to the Criminal Code.
The Criminal Code of Canada, as I said previously, states that we must not promote hatred against an identifiable group and that this group is identified by means of colour, race, religion or ethnic origin and I propose to add one word, the word "age". In other words, under this new definition, if you promote hatred against an identifiable age group, that would also be an offence as well as promoting hatred against someone because of their colour, because of their race, because of their origin and so forth. To promote hatred against a specific age group would then be an offence under the Criminal Code.
Just relating back to the cards in question, just in case anyone is unsure whether this amendment would in fact accomplish the objective, I want to state to you, Madam Speaker, that the children in question all appear to me to be within the age group of roughly a few months to three or four years. It is quite easy for anyone to determine
that what the cards promote in fact is, in my opinion, hatred against very young children and I do believe that the amendment that I am proposing would correct the situation.
At the very least, I am sure that those who export this product into Canada and those who import it, those who purchase it here, once this amendment is passed, would be quite reluctant to attempt to import the product or even for those who sell it to people across the border would be reluctant to selling it because of course they know that they could potentially be charged for a breach of the Criminal Code of Canada.
I know that the number of private members' bills that is passed in this Parliament in any given year is, shall we say, small to say the least. Only a handful of bills do make it. I am asking colleagues on all sides of the House today to set aside any differences that we might have for the good of our children.
We are opening today this United Nations conference on children. We could in a very small way make a contribution this afternoon, in the few minutes that this House has to sit before adjourning for the weekend. I propose that we adopt this bill at second reading. In the event that there is a minor change to be performed, or course the committee that would be studying the bill clause by clause is well equipped to do that. It would do so if given the opportunity. That opportunity of course is contingent upon this House not talking the bill out, in other words, this House adjourning the debate prior to three o'clock in order to permit the vote.
Naturally, it is my hope that members on all sides of the House would vote in support of this private member's bill, a bill to end hatred against children, or at least in a small way improve that condition.
Madam Speaker, I believe I have one or two minutes left and I just want to indicate to you that I have received correspondence from people right across the country on this issue. I will read a letter sent to me by E. M. Zaleski of Windsor, Ontario which states, and I read selectively:
Dear Mr. Boudria:
I was particularly pleased to read about your stand to ban thebubble gum cards "Garbage Pail Kids" with their sick advertising from being sold in Canada, since I, myself, have just written a letter to the president of Topps Chewing Gum Inc., complaining of the grossness of their cards. I enclose a copy of this letter.
September 28, 1990

This is a letter I received from Windsor. I have another letter which I received from Mrs. Maiy Hawes of Calgary, Alberta which states:
Last night my granddaughter showed me a collection of "Garbage Pail Kids" and 1 nearly threw up. You are right to say these cards should not be allowed in Canada.
I could read on and on from the stack of letters that I have here. Individual Canadians are not the only ones who have written to me on this issue. I just want to read to you a short excerpt from a resolution passed by the Peterborough County Board of Education on November 25, 1988 in which they adopted the following resolution:
WHEREAS the Topps Chewing Gum Inc. product called 'Garbage Pail Kids' is most objectionable and is contrary to the values taught in our public schools, and
WHEREAS this product is available in retail outlets throughout Ontario,
I will just read the conclusion:
Therefore, be it resolved that the Ontario Public School Boards' Association petition Topps Chewing Gum Inc., the Federal Ministry of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and the Provincial Ministry of Consumer and Corporate Relations to have these products withdrawn.
Clearly, Canadians do not want this product. [Translation]
Madam Speaker, we know that children buy these cards. But even if they have the opportunity to do so, we parents have to guide them and stop them from buying them. Of course we all know that if you give loose change to a child going to the convenience store he will not necessarily return with what you expect. We know they can buy whatever is on the shelves. For the same reason, we do not want our children to buy pornographic material in convenience stores.
I think we all hope our children will never again be able to buy this kind of hate products aimed at other children. These products lower the value of human life, so I urge all my colleagues to support me with a view to banning them as soon as possible.

maintopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   CRIMINAL CODE MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, at the outset of my remarks I want to join my House of Commons colleagues who, a few seconds ago, congratulated the member from Glengarry-Prescott-Russell for his initiative. In response to his invitation of a moment ago I can tell him that government members on
Private Members' Business
this side of the House do not intend to take a partisan approach to this issue. I hardly think the matter raised by my colleague from Glengariy-Prescott-Russell will prompt members to express diverging views because they are Liberals, New Democrats or Progressive Conservatives. There can be no partisan politics when dealing with such issues. As far as we are concerned, at least, there is no point of view which stems from ideology as such. The question raised by our colleague is of some concern to many Canadians.
We all know that in recent years the courts had to rule in a few hate propaganda cases. The Keegstra case in Alberta immediately comes to mind as do those of Andrews and Smith in Ontario where these cases went all the way to the superior courts. I believe that at this very moment, the Supreme Court is being asked to judge in this connection on the constitutionality of certain sections of the Criminal Code, including subsection 319(2). This means, Madam Speaker, that the subject raised by the hon. member here in the House today is now being considered by our courts and by the Supreme Court of Canada, specifically with respect to the Keegstra, Andrews and Smith cases.
I also want to join the hon. member in condemning this kind of propaganda-let's call it propaganda, he used the word-which some people see as "entertainment". Quotation marks are indeed in order here because personally, I see no redeeming features in the kind of illustrations on the cards being sold to children. I tried be objective and see whether there was anything positive here but quite frankly, I cannot, and that includes the product itself.
I don't think extensive research is necessaiy, Madam Speaker. I don't think anyone will order a doctorate thesis on the subject. I think any reasonable person will agree it is not the kind of product we want to sell or make available to children.
One wonders about the motives of the people who distribute and about the kind of person that would have the guts to create this kind of product. It raises a number of questions that are quite troubling for us and for all members of this House.
Madam Speaker, I would like to speak very briefly about the present provisions in the Criminal Code on this subject, and which have been there for some time.

September 28, 1990
Private Members' Business
First of all, hate propoganda is an offence that is defined under Common Law. Under our legal system, however people are not prosecuted under Common Law but our Criminal Code is based on Common Law. People are prosecuted for offences that are specifically defined or codified the Criminal Code.
This is one of the principles of our criminal law. Law professors tell us you can do anything in Canada, provided there is no law against it. That is one of the first things you learn at law school, in criminal law. Therefore, this problem, and the hon. member was right to remind us, must be considered within the context of the Criminal Code.
The current provisions of the Criminal Code stem from a study which was carried out in 1965. In January of that year, Hon. Guy Favreau, the then minister of Justice, had appointed a Special Committee to study and report upon the problems related to the dissemination of hate propaganda in Canada.
This Committee, also known as the Cohen Committee, completed its study in 1965 and recommended a number of amendments to the Criminal Code. Anxious to harmonize the new legislation with the major tenets of the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide, as well as the International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination, and in line with the Cohen Committee recommendations, Parliament included in 1965 in the Criminal Code a number of provisions concerning hate propaganda.
If I mention these international conventions, Madam Speaker, it is because there is a close relationship between the current provisions of our Criminal Code and the provisions of International Law as it existed at the time.
These provisions deal with advocating genocide, public incitement of hatred, and wilful promotion of hatred. Section 318 of the Criminal Code criminalizes advocating genocide. Everyone who advocates genocide is liable to imprisonment for a term not exceeding five years. No proceeding for an offense under this section may be instituted without the consent of the Attorney General of Canada.
Madam Speaker, I wish to emphasize that these are exceptional provisions. This is not the kind of provisions
which we find in most of the offences mentioned in the Criminal Code. There is a reason for that. In fact, in the case of hate propaganda, an additional review is required. Before legal action can be taken, there must be a political examination, so to speak-and again, I use quotation marks-but there must also be a political will to act before charges can be brought.
In other words, at this level the persons must be committed to suing the person or persons concerned or the organization, according to the values stated or judged, or the prevailing circumstances.
The subsection 319 (1) of the Criminal Code mentions the people publicly inciting hatred. The base of the offence is the incitation to hatred in a public place-and this is the important part of the article-in a way "likely to lead to a breach of the peace" The term "public place" is defined in the Code as including any place to which the public has access as of right or by invitation, express or implied". Those who break the law in this regard are liable to imprisonment for a term not exceeding two years.
The subsection 319 (2) of the Code covers the case of persons who, by communicating statement, wilfully promote hatred.
This violation differs from the previously mentioned one in that it is not necessary for the wrongdoing to be likely to lead to a breach of the peace. Moreover, the statements must be communicated other than in private conversation. Because there are limits to what the legislator can do and to what we can do as a society, Madam Speaker, I think that common sense would dictate that we at least not seek to regulate in that matter. Private conversations should not be regulated either. That is pure common sense.
As regards the latter violation, Parliament adopted means of ensuring freedom of expression is protected for, in our society, Madam Speaker, every individual liberty is measured against the liberty of others. Let us not forget that freedom of expression, as described in the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, in section 2 b) of the Charter in particular, is what serves to counterbalance these provisions of the Criminal Code prohibiting hate propaganda.
September 28, 1990

The definition of "identifiable group"-and I think that is the key of the problem-which would be modified by my hon. colleague's bill, applies to the three offenses I have just mentioned.
Madam Speaker, I think it is obvious based on the historical background of the provisions relating to hate propaganda, that these provisions were originally intended and are still intended to protect visible minorities, religious groups and ethnic minorities in Canada. The underlying principle of the Report of the Special Committee on Hate Propaganda in Canada on which the present provisions on hate propaganda are based-and I am about to conclude, Madam Speaker-was to provide better protection for minority groups against racism, antisemitism and religious intolerance.
Madam Speaker, that is what in legal circles is called the genus of an article or argument-in other words, a definition that is used to achieve a specific purpose. What the hon. member is proposing today is a definition that goes beyond the genus. That is why the government does not see this particular amendment, at least not in its present form, as the ideal solution to the problem described by the hon. member. It may be the answer later on. However, at this time, Madam Speaker, we believe that the problem described by the hon. member could be dealt with more effectively other than by adding to a section that is now being challenged before the Supreme Court of Canada. My point is that in the next few months, the Supreme Court will have to rule on the validity of all these sections and at that time will decide what the law will be. Furthermore, in a context that is rather technical, it may not be the ideal solution to include age in a definition that cannot suitably include this factor.
That is why, Madam Speaker, I think that as legislators we must act prudently and wait a few months until we have a judgment by the Supreme Court of Canada, which we can then use to propose to Canadians an effective and lasting solution to the very important problem raised by the hon. member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell.

maintopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   CRIMINAL CODE MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I join with others in commending my colleague from Glengarry-Prescott-Russell on his initiative on this most
Private Members' Business
important and critical matter. I join with my colleague from the Conservative Party who has just spoken and say that indeed this is non-partisan. This is not a political issue. It is an issue of compassion and caring where we, as Members of Parliament, are attempting to do something to rid this country of hate propaganda levied against children.
My hon. friend from the Conservative Party has indicated that we should see this in the context of amendments to the Criminal Code. That is one context, but I suggest there is another.
This weekend the Prime Minister will be co-hosting the United Nations World Summit for Children on behalf of Canada. While there is a lot of cynicism in terms of our Prime Minister, would it not be a perfect signal for the Parliament of Canada on the eve of the UN World Summit for Children to agree to refer this matter of hate propaganda levied against children to the appropriate committee for consideration in terms of dealing with this issue? I will be the first to say that perhaps this is not the best way to deal with it. At least it is a way. That forms another context in which I think we should examine this whole issue. We are only too familiar with the fact that children grow up today in an atmosphere of violence, violence that is demonstrated by their daily and weekly viewing of television. If you watch television, as a normal child in our country probably does, you see hundreds of killings every month on television. That rips the status of human life in terms of the image of the child.
We tune in to television in our homes now at certain times of the day and in some cases all day long to pornographic films, soft pom, hard pom, so any child now who can turn the dial on a television set can view some pretty interesting television to say the least, to say nothing of the rap tapes, discs, and records that one buys, that children tend to buy, and to listen to the messages that are sent out on those tapes, discs and casettes is something disgusting.
This is the context in which children today are being raised. It has been brought to our attention that these bubble gum packages imported from the United States carry these little pictures of kids that are supposed to be entertaining, as my hon. friend indicated. These are pictures of children with their heads cut off, pictures of

Private Members' Business
children hanging from trees-lynched, if you like, Madam Speaker-where their hands are being burned in boiling water, where they are being ripped open with a knife, where their legs are being chopped off, where their stomachs are being ripped open, where their backs are being lacerated, where they are being run over by vehicles, where they are being twisted to death in the form of torture.
I can go on and on, but I think the point is well made. These are disgusting. This is not something that I think anyone would suggest is entertaining for a young person. Yet you can buy these in any shop in our communities.
I am sure all of us have received representations from parent groups, school groups and individuals coming to our offices, saying that this is coming into Canada. This is not right.
Well, as parliamentarians we ask what can be done. Surely we just cannot sit back and say that the existing Criminal Code does not allow us to do anything, just sit back and accept this.
What can we do? Well my hon. friend from Glengarry-Prescott-Russell has come up with a suggestion. That is that we have regulations in the Criminal Code that does not allow hate propaganda against certain groups, and he has mentioned them, based on cult groups, based on colour, sex, creed, religion, country of origin. So we are able then to combat this type of hate propaganda that is aimed at those particular groups.
But we have nothing too prohibitive in that same way for hate propaganda that is destined against children.
This very simple Private Member's Bill attempts to include the wording of an identifiable age group as part of the criteria where hate propaganda can be brought into the courts under the Criminal Code of Canada.
I think this is a great initiative. It is at least an initiative, Madam Speaker. I become worried when I hear my hon. friend from the Conservative Party say there must be better ways to deal with this and so we will leave it for now.
I think it is perfect that on the eve of the United Nations World Summit for Children that the House of Commons would take this initiative. We all admit that this may not be the answer, but to simply refer this to the appropriate committee to indicate, first of all, our
intention, our support for this initiative, and our disgust at this type of hate propaganda against children in our country, is a very laudable initiative.
We all know the rules here. If the debate ceases before the hour hand reaches three o'clock, this will then be put to a vote. I will say, representing the New Democratic Party, that we would vote in favour of this initiative. I have heard from my friends in the Liberal Party who say they will support this initiative. All eyes will be on the Conservative Party to see whether they support this initiative.
If they do, we will simply have a voice vote and the whole matter is referred to the appropriate committee. Simple, clean, and one of the most positive initiatives this House could take at the end of a very, very chaotic week in the House of Commons.
On behalf of my colleagues in the New Democratic Party, I want to say we support this initiative. We are abhorred at the kind of hate literature that is coming into our country from the United States. It is disgusting in all ways and forms. If this initiative can prevent this type of hate literature from getting into the hands of our children, we will be taking a step in the right direction.
I encourage all my colleagues to stop this debate well before three o'clock to advance this initiative.

maintopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   CRIMINAL CODE MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   CRIMINAL CODE MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is my privilege and honour to support my colleague who brought this bill before the House.
To me there are not enough words in the English language to say just how evil are these cards by the name of Garbage Pail Kids. They are vile, repugnant, and against everything that is decent and humane about our society. For people who distribute them to say that they distribute them because children like them and want to buy them is to be totally irresponsible.
If we listen to the evidence of so many children who live in poverty in this country today, they will tell us in as many words that they feel like garbage, that their peers call them garbage, and that adults treat them like garbage. We cannot tolerate and allow this type of propaganda, this type of reverse sensitization to exist in our country.
September 28, 1990

We are judged by what we do not do as often as by what we do. Good people often fail to do what they must do. What we lack so much in this country today is leadership. Again I just want to applaud my colleague for taking the initiative at this very important point in time in bringing forward this proposed legislation. I do not want to take up a lot of time because I want to ensure that this legislation is passed in this House this afternoon by voice vote.
Last night on national television, on the CBC program The Journal, we watched the story of the plight of children world-wide, children who are treated so indecently, like garbage. In some nations of the world today, because children are considered as garbage, they go about killing children on the street. We have to stop. We have to take the opportunity to turn the tide back and do something to address the very dire straits in which children around the world and in Canada find themselves. We must take the initiative as responsible adults to speak out on their behalf. Even though some children because of their age may think that this is amusing, the children that it hurts have no voice in this country. They depend upon us to speak up on their behalf.
I support my colleague's bill. I would urge and expect all of us to affirm it in a vote this afternoon.

maintopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   CRIMINAL CODE MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I will make my remarks quickly so that we can get to the vote. I want to thank my hon. colleague, the hon. member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell, for his determined and thoughtful initiative.
What we see here is nothing more than an housekeeping matter in the Criminal Code. He wants to add the word age. In fact it would arm the government minister with the necessary tool to prevent the proliferation of this kind of horrendous material. It is hate propaganda. There is no question of that.
We have these bubble gum cards, produced by Topps Chewing Gum Incorporated, with pictures depicting babies and older children expressing pain and agony while under dissection or surprise at having been impaled by the horn of a unicorn. This serves no one and in fact is nothing short of sick.
Private Members' Business
Where do we stop? What do we see next? Will we maybe see elderly persons? Will they pick up elderly persons and start making a mockery of them in this kind of disgusting material?
Given that the municipalities and school boards have condemned the product, it remains incumbent upon us to support them. I would hope that the House would adjourn debate on this motion to allow us to vote and vote in the affirmative in support of the member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell and Bill C-207 and, in the process, to denounce this product and any product like it.

maintopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   CRIMINAL CODE MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I want to commence by letting the hon. member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell know that I think he has undertaken today to put before parliamentarians an issue that demands our attention and requires our sensitivities. I am one who having looked upon this legislation believes that there are some technical inadequacies to it and that in some parts, perhaps in its greatest failing, does not go far enough.
I pondered as I heard the hon. member read through a list of categories of people which he says the present legislation would restrict from hate literature and then point out that age was not one of those categories. If I heard him correctly, I did not note either that gender was one of those categories. It would seem to me that a further and more thorough examination ought to be undertaken with respect to a number of these criteria.
I believe that there would be a lot of advantage for this House in some ways in waiting for the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada with respect to the hearing of the Keegstra case and its pronouncements on hate literature to give us a durable kind of resolution that we might undertake.
Having said that, none of us in any corner of this Chamber would ever want to be in a situation where it would appear that for some reason we were not able to stand up, not only for an age that are called children but for an age that is called innocent. These criteria in my judgment are not as thorough as I would like and not as extensive as I would like. There are some technical limitations to them, particularly on a weekend when we stand on the eve of a world conference being held in New York to recognize the plight of children around the

Private Members' Business
world. The descriptions thereof are well beyond the imagination of the majority of Canadians.
In the country of Brazil there exists today some 25 million street children. I remember that statistic with ease and with pain, because it is exactly the same number of street children as the total population of Canada located in one country. Street children are children who wander loose and alone without their parents.
The hon. member puts before us the whole notion that there is coming into this country the kind of material he described. From the speeches I have heard from others, I can only recognize that they have seen that material also and I accept it as fact. I have not seen it, but I do not doubt it. All I know is that if it fits the descriptions I have heard, it is not in a context which is appropriate that we have that kind of material within our society.
I suppose, to repeat, what I sense is that we would be better off-I say that quite genuinely-to have done a more thorough examination of the matter. I believe that there are other categories of the question of hatred that ought to be examined.
I also believe it would have been far more prudent for us as parliamentarians to have moved after the Supreme Court completed its deliberations with respect to the Keegstra case and laid before us all its recommendations.
Because of the evidence the hon. member has laid before us and because of the inability of this sector of society to be able to stand to protect themselves, it is appropriate for us as parliamentarians to accept the amendments that the hon. member wants to send forward to committee stage. Perhaps at that time we can expand on them. I am not sure to what extent he sees it, but I would presume that we should be able to expand in some detail and into different dimensions.
If in that process we can find even a much better bill that is different enough to change the character and nature of the bill, I believe that the hon. member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell will have started an appropriate initiative. He will have forced officials to come forward with an appropriate total response.
If that leads to a different, fuller and more expanded piece of legislation than what is being proposed, so be it. Let's wish, at least as I sit down, that as they meet this weekend in New York we can become a planet that is
more caring for the young and is more intently interested in those who are unable to protect themselves.
Then we can stand on the right side of right, particularly in this case, in the interests of children who are being perpetrated upon by unholy material which in the final analysis can do nothing other than make all of us as a society stand together and say: "We repulse such information perpetrated upon our young."

maintopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   CRIMINAL CODE MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
I rise on a point of order, Madam Speaker. After having consulted with colleagues in the House, especially with the member from Glengarry- Prescott-Russell and the House leader of the New Democratic Party, I think Your Honour would find unanimous consent in this House at this time, after a very trying week of debates for Parliament, especially on the eve of the world summit on youth as my colleague from Crowfoot and others have mentioned.
This would be a good opportunity for the House to offer its unanimous consent so that this subject matter could be sent to a legislative committee for study. We could take into consideration all the arguments that were brought before this House today and take into consideration all the elements that will be coming into play in the next few months. Then the House of Commons and the government together will deal with this issue in the most efficient manner as possible.

speakerposition: Liberal Party Deputy House Leader; Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
maintopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   CRIMINAL CODE MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I confirm that there has been such a discussion. As I understand it, you will require unanimous consent, first, to withdraw the bill and, second, to ask that the subject matter be referred to the appropriate parliamentary committee. Given that the House seems to be favourably disposed to that, I want to thank everybody even if they are not disposed to it.
I cannot presume that such consent has been achieved. We will have to you, Madam Speaker, to ask the House if it is so disposed. If such consent is achieved, I will thank hon. members in advance for their co-operation.

maintopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   CRIMINAL CODE MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I too want to confirm that the discussions have occurred. This is a wonderful way to culminate a week. It has not been an easy week for anybody, but I cannot think of a more appropriate way to end it off than to withdraw the bill and send the subject matter to the appropriate committee. It advances the initiative taken by the hon. member for Glengarry- Prescott-Russell.

I want to say on behalf of the New Democratic Party that we are pleased with the element of co-operation we have seen for the first time this week, almost for the first time this year. Again I say to my colleagues in the House of Commons that this is a very positive initiative with which to end the week.

maintopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   CRIMINAL CODE MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Madam Speaker, first I should like to set the record straight: they say everybody was consulted and there is general agreement, but I can tell you that such is not the case and that nobody in this House speaks for me. The fact is, given the obvious merit of this motion and exceptionally, I will co-operate with the members for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell and Sherbrooke precisely because we are talking about the future of our children. This, however, should not be taken as a precedent.

maintopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   CRIMINAL CODE MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Hear, hear.

Private Members' Business
